summary.summary: Camden took no new borrowing in 2025/26 and held external debt flat at £294m (£169m PWLB at 4.57%, £124m LOBOs at 4.43%, £1m community bond), but its CFR jumped £50m to £812m, pushing under-borrowing (capital spend financed from its own cash instead of loans) to £518m. The council says this internal borrowing saves about £10.4m a year versus borrowing at current rates, but also that planned use of earmarked reserves will create an external borrowing requirement within 12-24 months, and that investments were drawn down in-year to support cash flow as service demand outpaced funding. Headline investments of £197m flatter the picture: £159m of that is held on behalf of the North London Waste Authority. The report itself flags a greater likelihood that LOBO lenders will exercise their rate-reset options as market rates have risen. A £6.4m loan was made in April 2025 to wholly-owned Camden Living Housing Association; all prudential indicators were met.

signals.headline: £124m of LOBO loans (average rate 4.43%, average life ~25 years); council states higher market rates make lender rate-reset calls more likely, with repayment at par the fallback
signals.why: A called LOBO would force Camden to refinance or repay a slice of £124m at today's much higher rates, exactly when its cash buffer is being run down.

signals.headline: Investments drawn down in 2025/26 to support cash flow and service delivery; planned earmarked-reserve usage expected to create an external borrowing requirement within 12-24 months on top of £518m under-borrowing
signals.why: The cheap internal-borrowing strategy ends when the reserves funding it are spent, converting a deferred liability into real borrowing at ~6% PWLB rates.

signals.headline: £6.4m loan advanced 24 April 2025 to wholly-owned Camden Living Housing Association to buy 34 social-rent homes, with about 10 more purchases planned
signals.why: Council cash is now exposed to a housing subsidiary's ability to service debt from social rents.

compliance.notes: A strong, well-evidenced inner-London TMSS. Strongest on the prudential/treasury indicators and MRP: capital plans, CFR, gross-debt-vs-CFR and financing-cost ratios are all multi-year (2024/25 actual to 2028/29), split GF/HRA and reconciled; the liability benchmark is charted to 2064/65; the investment/creditworthiness strategy prioritises security-liquidity-yield and drives rating-based counterparty limits and durations using CDS/market data beyond ratings; and the MRP policy is comprehensive, asset-life-justified and full-council approved. Weakest area is the commercial/non-treasury investment framework: no paragraphs 51-53 compliance statement (COM-02), no proportionality-to-financial-capacity demonstration (core COM-03 only partial), and no separate purpose-based reporting, IMPs, security/income-dependence disclosures, exit review or clear nil statement (COM-04/05/07/08/11 absent). Other notable gaps: no formal adoption of the CIPFA TM Code's four clauses (core GOV-01, only 'have regard to'); no explicit fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits (core RISK-02); no separate HRA/GF liability benchmark despite material HRA debt (LB-04); and minor omissions on sterling-only borrowing (BOR-03), audit-qualification flagging (RPT-05), derivatives policy (RISK-06) and segregation of duties (GOV-08). Scored from the Cabinet 25 Feb / Full Council 2 March 2026 report (CS/2026/08) and its Appendix 1 TMSS 2026/27; no separate capital strategy was read.

news_drafts.headline: Camden repays £29m LOBO loan after lender proposed 7.77%, replacing it with PWLB borrowing at 4.69%
news_drafts.lead:
Camden Council repaid a £29m bank loan on 27 August 2026 after the lender, FMS Wertmanagement, proposed raising its interest rate from 4.625% to 7.77%. The loan was a LOBO loan (a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher rate and the council may then repay in full instead of accepting it). The council's Audit and Corporate Governance Committee, meeting on 24 September, received the details in a treasury management update (a report on how the council borrows and manages its cash).

FMS notified the council of the proposed rise on 20 August. The council used its right to repay rather than accept. On 2 September it took out a replacement £29m loan for two years from the PWLB (Public Works Loan Board, the government's lending arm for councils) at 4.69%, a rate that includes a discount for its housing revenue account (the ring-fenced account for council homes). The paper puts the new loan's interest at about £1.360m a year, which it says avoids about £893,000 a year compared with the FMS rate. It costs about £19,000 a year more than the original loan did.

The paper lists three more FMS loans with lender option dates: £15m on 24 September, £25m on 9 October and £10m on 29 October, £50m in all. It says further borrowing or refinancing (replacing old loans with new ones) may be needed during 2026/27, depending on "lender decisions, cash flow requirements, capital financing obligations, and prevailing interest rates".

findings.headline: The Council faces three further FMS LOBO lender option dates totalling £50m scheduled for September-October 2026.
findings.detail: FMS has notified the Council of additional lender option dates on 24 September 2026 (£15m), 9 October 2026 (£25m), and 29 October 2026 (£10m). The Council notes that depending on 'lender decisions, cash flow requirements, capital financing obligations, and prevailing interest rates', further borrowing or refinancing activity may be required during 2026/27.
findings.matters: £50m in potential refinancing decisions over six weeks indicates ongoing LOBO repricing exposure and material forward visibility of borrowing costs and decisions for 2026/27.
findings.figures: £15m due 24 September 2026; £25m due 9 October 2026; £10m due 29 October 2026
findings.quote: There are further FMS loans due for call during 2026/27: 24 September 2026 – £15m, 9 October 2026 – £25m, 29 October 2026 – £10m

findings.headline: FMS Wertmanagement exercised its lender option with a proposed rate increase to 7.77% on a £29m LOBO loan; the council repaid at par on 27 August 2026 and replaced it with PWLB borrowing at 4.69%, avoiding £893,000 in annual costs.
findings.detail: On 20 August 2026, FMS notified the Council of a proposed rate increase from 4.625% to 7.77% on its £29m LOBO loan (Loan Instrument Number 640722AI). The Council exercised its borrower option to repay the loan in full rather than accept the revised rate. The loan and accrued interest were repaid on 27 August 2026. On 2 September 2026, the Council took out a replacement £29m PWLB loan at 4.69% (inclusive of HRA discount) for a two-year term. This refinancing avoided approximately £893,000 in annual interest costs compared with accepting the FMS rate, though it increased annual costs by approximately £19,000 compared to the original FMS rate.
findings.matters: A material LOBO refinancing event with significant cost outcomes demonstrates prudent rate benchmarking and has material implications for 2026/27 debt service budgets.
findings.figures: £29m loan; FMS proposed rate 7.77% (from 4.625%); PWLB replacement rate 4.69%; annual cost avoidance £893,000; annual cost increase versus original FMS rate £19,000
findings.quote: By comparison, the replacement PWLB loan will incur annual interest costs of approximately £1.360 million per annum, resulting in an annual cost avoidance of approximately £893,000.

findings.headline: Government funding for affordable housing remains uncertain post-2025 Spending Review
findings.detail: Following the 2025 Spending Review, Camden is awaiting government detail on support for affordable housing delivery. Officers will review options including low-cost borrowing, but the level of funding available is not yet confirmed. This creates uncertainty for the existing Camden Living programme, which has already committed £6.4m to acquire 34 affordable homes with a further 10 expected.
findings.matters: Affordable housing is a stated priority but future delivery depends on government funding that is currently unconfirmed. If support is lower than expected, the council may need additional borrowing or will need to reduce housing targets.
findings.figures: £6.4m already lent to Camden Living Housing Association for 34 homes, further 10 expected
findings.quote: Following the Spending Review 2025, the Council is awaiting further detail on Government support for affordable housing delivery. Officers will continue to review funding opportunities, including the potential use of low-cost borrowing

findings.headline: Borrowing requirement expected to materialise within 12-24 months as reserves deplete
findings.detail: The council's long-term financial modelling indicates that gradual depletion of earmarked reserves will trigger an external borrowing requirement within the next 12-24 months. This marks the timeline when the under-borrowing liability will convert into actual debt issuance and when the council will need to access debt markets.
findings.matters: Lenders should monitor for when Camden enters debt markets for this funding. The scale and timing of this borrowing will depend on how quickly reserves deplete and on market interest rates at that time.
findings.figures: Borrowing requirement expected within 12-24 months, projected CFR growth
findings.quote: Current long-term financial modelling indicates a gradual and planned usage of earmarked reserves which will reduce cash balances and is expected to create a borrowing requirement within the next 12 to 24 months.

findings.headline: Structural funding gap eroding reserves: rising demand and costs outpacing grant income
findings.detail: Camden is drawing down reserves to bridge a structural gap between rising service demand and stagnant grant funding. The council explicitly reports that 'demand for services has continued to increase, while expenditure has risen and funding from grants and other income sources has not kept pace.' A significant proportion of investments were utilised during 2025/26 to support cash flow and meet service delivery requirements, reducing total investments held. This is not a one-time issue but an ongoing structural imbalance.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing operational gaps is unsustainable and constrains future financial flexibility. Lenders need to understand whether this gap is temporary or a permanent structural problem driven by government funding cuts or rising service costs.
findings.figures: Investment portfolio £197m at 31 March 2026 (reduced from prior year), proportion of investments drawn down to support cash flow
findings.quote: Demand for services has continued to increase, while expenditure has risen and funding from grants and other income sources has not kept pace.
